item.title: AdsorbML: How AI Is Transforming Catalyst Discovery for Clean Energy and Chemicals
item.content:encoded: Researchers developed AdsorbML, a hybrid AI + physics method that finds the best way molecules bind to catalyst surfaces—critical for designing fuels and chemicals. Using machine-learning potentials with selective Density Functional Theory calculations, the system identifies optimal adsorption energies ~2,000× faster than traditional approaches. The team also released the Open Catalyst 2020-Dense Dataset, a benchmark with ~100,000 configurations to standardize catalyst discovery research.

item.title: Facebook Echo Chambers Are Real But They May Not Be Driving Polarization
item.content:encoded: A massive field experiment led by researchers including Brendan Nyhan and Matthew Gentzkow analyzed how echo chambers affect political views on Facebook. In a study of 23,377 users during the 2020 United States presidential election, the platform reduced exposure to politically like-minded posts by one-third. While users saw slightly more opposing content and less misinformation, their political attitudes and polarization levels didn’t change.

item.title: Why Eigenvalues are the Key to Solving AI Hallucinations
item.content:encoded: Early AI development relied heavily on scaling neural networks without fully understanding how they worked internally. Researchers are now turning to the spectral properties of linear algebra—particularly eigenvalues and eigenvectors—to better interpret how neural networks process information. By studying the geometry of latent space and identifying meaningful circuits inside transformer models, scientists can isolate and enhance specific capabilities such as reasoning or coding. Hardware innovations are also emerging to accelerate these complex calculations. Ultimately, spectral techniques like normalization may help stabilize AI systems and reduce hallucinations, marking a shift from brute-force scaling toward mathematically guided “spectral intelligence.”

item.title: Java Under the Hood - Dive Into JVM Memory Model and Garbage Collector
item.content:encoded:
Java abstracts away manual memory management, but the JVM still operates on a precise memory model. Local variables and method frames live on the stack, while actual objects live on the heap, which is divided into generations to make garbage collection efficient. Different reference types (strong, soft, weak, phantom) influence GC behavior, especially for caches and off-heap resources. Garbage Collection uses variations of mark-and-sweep to identify reachable objects and reclaim memory from the rest, sometimes compacting to avoid fragmentation. GC pauses are real and can impact latency, which is why selecting the right collector matters (G1, Parallel, ZGC, Shenandoah, etc.) and why JVM tuning exists. Understanding how memory works under the hood enables developers to diagnose leaks, reduce allocation pressure, tune pause times, and configure the JVM for different workloads — turning memory management from a black box into a performance tool.
